To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

Alu and mouse B1 elements are selectively retained in the regulatory regions of specific functional classes and that these elements have spread in the human and mouse genomes in a manner that is consistent with positive selection.
Alu and/or B1 repeats have been selectively retained upstream and intronically in the genes of specific functional classes.
Alu and mouse B1 repeats have been selectively retained, rather than lost, in the upstream and the intronic regions of specific gene functional classes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the evolutionary forces acting on Alu and B2 elements and their functional consequences.
the evolutionary forces that have shaped the distribution of Alu and other SINE elements, and we have discovered a novel class of functional links between SINE elements and genes.
the evolutionary history and the functional role of the Alu and B2 elements, which are the most abundant transposable elements in the primate genome.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Alu and, to a lesser extent, B1 elements have not been lost, but rather have been retained, in the upstream and/or intronic regions of specific functional classes.
Alu and mouse B1 repeats are the result of both positive and negative selection, but the latter has been much less effective in removing these elements from the genome.
the Alu and B 1 elements are the results of positive selection.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Alu and B-1 repeats, which have spread in a seemingly random fashion, are not random at all.
Alu and, to a lesser extent, B1 elements are preferentially found in the upstream and/or intronic regions of a subset of functional classes.

Alu and other mobile elements, contrary to the prevalent belief, have not spread randomly in our genome, and that the extant copies of these elements in our genomes are the result of selective retention rather than selective loss.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the distribution of Alu and, to a lesser extent, of B1 repeats is not the result of a random process, but instead is the result of a complex evolutionary mechanism that has shaped the distribution of these elements in a way that is consistent with their current function.

the distribution of Alu and other repetitive sequences across the genome is not the result of a random process, but is shaped by selective forces that have favored the retention of these elements in specific genomic regions.
Alu and, to a lesser extent, B1 elements have a functional role in specific classes of genes, and that their distribution is shaped by positive selection.
